text.title: Design Docs at Big Tech Companies Core Rules
text.summary: 5 testable rules every Design Docs at Big Tech Companies application must enforce. These are HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them. Folds in two former files. How Google, Amazon, Uber, Spotify, Stripe, Meta, and Microsoft structure design documents, reviews, and decision records — with key distinguishing features per company. Decision table for when a design doc is required; LLM assistance effectiveness by task type; common mistakes; and agent-specific gotchas. The common mistakes now live in `content/03-failure-modes.xml`.

rule.statement: Design doc MUST exist before implementation PR opens. Match document weight to change scope; write before coding, never after.
rule.rationale: Doc-after-code is rationalisation, not design. Post-implementation documentation defeats the purpose — design docs exist to catch issues when changes are still cheap.

rule.statement: Doc weight MUST match decision scope (≤4 pages team, ≤6 pages cross-org, ≤10 pages company-wide).
rule.rationale: Heavy docs for small scope kill momentum; light docs for big scope miss alternatives.

rule.statement: Alternatives section MUST include 'do nothing' with rationale. Always include "do nothing" as Alternative 1 in the alternatives section.
rule.rationale: Without 'do nothing', the doc is advocacy, not analysis. Sometimes the best decision is not to build. Forcing this option ensures the author justifies why building is worth the cost and risk.

rule.statement: Every doc MUST set a review deadline when circulated.
LLM may draft prose but MUST NOT author the alternatives section; humans pick alternatives.
rule.rationale: LLM alternatives default to strawmen. The two folded sources disagree with this rule: r9-llm-structure-not-accuracy and r10-llm-alternatives-cap allow LLM alternative brainstorming. Until reconciled, this rule governs — an LLM may brainstorm candidates as input, but the alternatives section is picked and written by a human.

rule.statement: Write in narrative prose, no bullet points, maximum 6 pages; supporting data goes in an unlimited appendix.
rule.rationale: Dense prose forces the author to synthesize; bullets permit loose thinking. Every word must carry information. Applies when the Amazon 6-pager format is the chosen doc_format; the page cap coincides with r2's cross-org budget.

rule.statement: Use the lightest template that fits the change scope; do not over-engineer the process.
rule.rationale: Uber evolved from simple RFCs to tiered ERDs precisely because heavyweight process for lightweight changes slows teams without adding value. r2-weight-matches-scope sets the page budget; this rule picks the template tier (listed under Uber tiered ERD below).

rule.statement: Separate the RFC (consensus-reaching) from the ADR (decision-recording); do not conflate the two jobs in one document.
rule.rationale: An RFC trying to reach consensus and record the decision simultaneously produces a document that does neither well. The RFC is collaborative and iterative; the ADR is the immutable record.

rule.statement: Use LLMs for initial structure, alternative brainstorming, and prose refinement; require human validation for every technical accuracy claim.
rule.rationale: LLMs generate plausible but technically inaccurate design docs when system-specific context is absent. Technical accuracy is the one dimension where LLM effectiveness is Low-Medium. Brainstorming feeds the human-authored alternatives section; r5-llm-assist-limit governs the section itself.

rule.statement: Limit LLM-generated alternatives to 2-3 concrete options; agents over-generate when not constrained.
rule.rationale: 5+ alternatives overwhelm reviewers and dilute focus. The value is in comparing 2-3 realistic options, not exhaustively listing all possibilities.

section.title: Company practices
section.p: Design documents serve four universal purposes: early issue identification (cheap to fix on paper), consensus building, knowledge sharing, and onboarding. Each company developed its own format based on culture and scale.

list.item: Google: informal Google Doc, inline comments, emphasis on "why" and trade-offs, always include "do nothing" alternative
Amazon: 6-Pager (narrative prose, no bullets, max 6 pages) + PR-FAQ (press release first, then FAQ); silent 20-25 min read at meeting start; "working backwards" from customer
Uber: RFC evolved to tiered ERD — Lightweight (team), Standard (cross-team), Heavyweight (org-wide); mailing list circulation with named approvers
Spotify: two-stage — RFC for consensus (1-3 weeks open), ADR for recording the decision; break large RFCs into big-picture + focused sub-RFCs
Stripe: strong written culture; RFCs for any decision needing cross-team alignment; high-bar async review; mentorship integrated
Meta/Facebook: notably less formal — no company-wide RFC process; 1-pagers optional; compensates with high talent bar and long tenures. Not recommended for most teams.
Microsoft: FDD (functional) + TDD (technical) integrated with Security Development Lifecycle (SDL); security is first-class, not afterthought
Shopify: GitHub PR-based RFC with explicit review deadline; deadline-driven consensus works well with agent-drafted PRs
Atlassian: Confluence-based, triad model (eng/PM/design), validated against architecture principles

section.p: Google process: author writes → shares with close collaborators → wider review → optional formal meeting → doc becomes historical artifact. No strict format, but common structure has emerged: Context and Scope, Goals and Non-Goals, Overview, Detailed Design, Alternatives Considered, Cross-cutting Concerns.

Amazon: PR-FAQ starts with a hypothetical press release announcing the finished product, then a FAQ document adding detail. This forces customer-centric thinking from day one. Meeting process: printed copies distributed, 20-25 minutes silent reading, discussion, printouts with handwritten notes returned to author.

list.item: Lightweight: team-only changes, mini RFC, team lead approver
Standard: cross-team impact, full RFC, multiple team approvers
Heavyweight: org/company-wide, detailed ERD, principal engineers
Bug fix: no doc needed
Small feature (1-2 days): optional 1-pager, team only
Medium feature (1-2 weeks): standard design doc, team + stakeholders
Large feature (1+ month): detailed RFC, cross-team review
Architecture change: RFC + ADR, company-wide
New service or system: full design doc, architecture review
API changes affecting consumers: yes
Database schema changes: yes
Security-sensitive changes: yes
High LLM effectiveness: initial structure from requirements, prose refinement, alternative brainstorming
Medium-High: risk identification, surface edge cases
Low-Medium: technical accuracy (requires expert validation)
Not applicable: organizational context, team history, stakeholder preferences, proprietary technology
